a5_ring: The socket ring is a dwarf chamber the size of a chapel, with the crown door in one wall and nine sockets set in a ring around it. Eight are filled and warm. The whole apparatus is in daily working use: there is a rota on the wall, a clerk's desk with a lamp on it, a scaffold on the frame and a gallery above with people standing at the rail.
e_a5_ring_1: The socket ring is seen, counted and left. The company walks nine miles back up a living gallery with a complete description of the crown door, a folder of certified copies, two irons that fit nothing here, and nothing done. Thane files the description. It is the best intelligence the Wardens have ever had and it changes nothing at all.
a5_sockets: At arm's length the ring resolves into detail: eight founding irons seated in eight warm sockets, each with a tally cut into its exposed face. The ninth socket is empty and worn bright around the mouth. In the floor in front of it there is a groove worn by nine hundred years of somebody standing in exactly one place.
a5_sockets_a: Eight tallies read at arm's length, one per iron, and they are not eight marks of ownership. They are eight parts of one instruction, and read in order they say exactly what the ninth iron is required to say and why. Ilsabet reads them twice and then puts her hand out for the company's own two irons.
a5_sockets_b: The ninth socket measured against Kar Duhn's iron and Hollowmarch's, with a wire and a straight edge. Both fit the socket's gauge. Neither fits its tally, which is cut for this door and no other. That tells the company precisely what the crown door will accept and precisely what it will not.
a5_sockets_c: A hand laid flat on the eighth iron's seating: warm, firm, and moving a sixteenth of an inch under the palm on the nine-count. The maintenance notes call that working properly. It is the first time in three books that anybody has touched one of these things while it was doing its job.
e_a5_sockets_1: An iron is drawn out of the crown ring on impulse while nobody appears to be looking, in a chamber that has been continuously staffed for nine hundred years. Nobody has ever needed to look. The ring itself keeps the count, and it registers a socket going empty considerably faster than any of the people in the room do.
e_a5_sockets_2: Eight tallies are read again in reverse order, which is not how they are meant to be read. The founders' plate says they must never be read that way, in a clause nobody in the counted city can translate. In reverse they are not a set of instructions. They are a sentence, and reading it aloud completes it.
a5_eighth: The eighth socket is the one the maintenance rota lists as due. Its iron stands a sixteenth proud of the collar. The stone collar around it is cracked in a curve, and a mason's chalk mark rings the crack with this week's date beside it, and the lead pot on the forge is already warm.
a5_eighth_a: A cracked collar packed with lead off the barrow by a company that has read the rota and can follow instructions. It takes an hour of unglamorous work with a ladle and a cold chisel. It is the single most useful hour anybody spends in this chamber, and the mason says so afterwards, twice.
a5_eighth_b: A chalk mark left alone and the mason's arrival waited for, which costs two hours. What it produces is a mason, his apprentice, and a conversation about the crack that changes the company's plan entirely, because he explains what the crack means and what it will do and how long the door has.
e_a5_eighth_1: The eighth iron is drawn to inspect a cracked collar, which is exactly the inspection the rota forbids, for exactly this reason. The collar goes the rest of the way as the iron clears it. The rota's wording, which nobody read to the end, was that the collar carries the iron and not the reverse.
a5_ninth: The ninth iron is in the chamber and not in the door: cut, tallied, and held in a rack under the keeper's own hand, waiting for the appointment of a hand to seat it. There is a plate above the rack. The rack has nine slots and eight are empty, and the ninth iron sits in the ninth slot.
a5_ninth_a: The crown iron off the rack and into a hand: founding gauge, cut with the crown tally, its flank filed blank where a name goes. The whole chamber's arithmetic turns, quietly and without any drama at all, toward whoever is holding it, and everybody in the room notices the turn including the people at the rail.
a5_ninth_b: The appointment plate, read above the rack: an office, a term of nine years, a set of duties in nine clauses, and a signature line. Across the signature line somebody has written the word held, in a hand that has been holding it for nineteen years, which is twice the term the plate specifies.
e_a5_ninth_1: The rack, the plate and the iron are all taken together, on the sound principle that evidence should be complete. That removes the entire appointment apparatus of a nine-hundred-year office in one movement. It also constitutes the appointment, because the apparatus is not a record of the office and never was.
a5_collar: Above the ring the door's collar plate is dwarf bronze with nine clauses on it: the founding specification of what this door is, what it holds, and what the nine hands are for. It is polished. It has been polished, on a rota, by people who cannot read it, for four hundred years.
a5_collar_a: Nine clauses read in full: containment, maintenance, the schedule, the hands, the arrears. Then clause nine, which describes what the founders expected to happen on the day the count stopped, and what they built into the door against that day. It is the most useful sentence anybody has read in three books.
e_a5_collar_1: A founding collar plate is prised off a door frame with a moor-iron pick, because it is the whole case and cases need exhibits. It is not a plaque. It is a fitting, and it has been holding the frame's upper collar into the rock since the founding, and the frame has been spreading since autumn.
a5_chair: The keeper's chair is a clerk's chair at a clerk's desk beside the ring, and it is occupied. The crown clerk of Kar Ashen is working through a delivery ledger by lamplight, nineteen years into a nine-year term. He looks up when the company comes in, and marks his place, and does not stand.
a5_chair_a: Two hours opposite a man who has kept a wyrm's accounts for nineteen years. He is courteous, exhausted and entirely lucid. He has been waiting nine years for a Warden company to sit down and ask him something, and when it happens he answers every question in order and asks for nothing in return.
a5_chair_b: A charter put on the crown clerk's desk, which he reads, initials and files in the correct box. Then he explains what it changes, which is nothing: the office is not a Warden appointment, has never been one, and the ring does not read charters. He says all of that without any satisfaction at all.
e_a5_chair_1: A knife is put down in front of the crown clerk of Kar Ashen. He looks at it. Then he goes on writing, because the one thing nineteen years in that chair has taught him is exactly how little a knife matters in this chamber, and he explains that too, while he writes, without looking up.
a5_signet: The keeper's signet lies on the desk beside the ledger: nine-sided, warm, sized for whoever picks it up. The initials of the last four holders have worn off the shank. There is a hollow in the desk's wood where it has sat, and the hollow is deeper than nineteen years of one man's work.
a5_signet_a: The signet taken off a working desk and put in a pocket rather than on a hand, which the crown clerk permits without comment. He enters it in his ledger as a transfer pending appointment, dates it, and then asks the captain to confirm the spelling of the company's name for the entry.
a5_signet_b: Four sets of initials read off a worn shank by lamplight. Three are meaningless. The fourth belongs to a Reckoning legate who came up to Sarnhold with a coach and a writ, and who is at this moment somewhere in this chamber, and who has therefore held this office before and put it down again.
e_a5_signet_1: A nine-sided signet is put on a finger to see whether it fits, and it fits exactly, as it has for nineteen holders. There is no ceremony. There has never been a ceremony. Putting it on is the appointment procedure in its entirety, which is written on the plate above the rack in the founders' hand.
a5_book: The crown ledger lies open on the desk: eleven hundred pages in nine hands, the current hand nineteen years old. There are four blank pages at the back. After them there is a ruled column with a heading, and the heading is for a tenth hand, and the ruling was done in the founders' century.
a5_book_a: Nine pages read over a clerk's shoulder: this month's deliveries, next month's notices, and a standing entry for the crown door's own maintenance signed by the same hand every ninth day. The maintenance entry has been signed nine hundred years without a gap, in nine hands, and every hand signed it personally.
e_a5_book_1: The crown ledger is taken off the desk of a working clerk. He allows it, and notes it, and hands over the pen with it. The company is now carrying the only document that can appoint or discharge a ninth hand, which means the appointment is now in the company's baggage rather than in the chamber.
a5_office: The office, explained by the man holding it: nine years' term, nine duties, a house in the counted city, a stipend paid quarterly, and a clause about what happens to the holder's household if the count is not kept. He explains the first four in a minute and takes eleven on the fifth.
a5_office_a: The household clause, explained without evasion: the holder's family stands as surety and is entered in the ninth column on appointment. It is removed from the column only when the successor's family is entered. His own family has been in it for nineteen years, which is why the term has not ended.
a5_office_b: The answer to why he took it: he was twenty-six, and the alternative was his sister taking it, and she had a child. The appointment plate had been on the rack for a month with the family's name already on it. He says all of that in about nine words and then goes back to the ledger.
e_a5_office_1: The crown clerk is asked whether he wants to be relieved of the office, and he answers yes, without hesitation, for the first time in nineteen years. Procedurally, that answer is the beginning of the appointment of whoever asked the question, and the plate above the rack sets out the rest of the procedure.
a5_voice: The door's own voice is not sound. It arrives in the chamber as arithmetic laid directly into five heads at once, and it opens by naming the company's dead: accurately, in order, with dates, including two that only one person in the company knows about. Then it waits, politely, for the company to catch up.
a5_voice_a: An offer heard out to its end, complete with term, rate, security and a clause about the frontier's peace. It is delivered with the patience of something that has made this offer to nine hands before and has all the time there is. It takes eleven minutes and it is entirely coherent.
a5_voice_b: A back turned on Ashendrel in its own socket chamber, which it accepts without any evident feeling. It stops addressing the captain. It does not stop, and the arithmetic continues to arrive, and it is now being addressed to whoever else in the company is still listening, and two of them are.
e_a5_voice_1: The account carried up from Gallowmere is read aloud in the socket chamber to the thing the account is about. Clause nine of the founders' plate describes that form of address specifically. It calls it an acknowledgement of the debt by a party competent to acknowledge it, and it explains what follows.
a5_terms: The terms, set out plainly enough that a clerk could minute them: the count ends today, the ring opens, the arrears of nine hundred years are paid in one payment out of what is nearest, and the frontier is free of the Compact forever afterwards. There is no trick in the wording. Everybody looks for one.
a5_terms_a: The terms written down word for word by a hedge-thaumaturge whose hand shakes for the first time in three books, witnessed by a Reckoning sister and sealed with a Warden charter's own seal. Whatever else happens now, the offer exists on paper, in the founders' form, in a court's language.
a5_terms_b: The question about nearest is asked and answered precisely, in figures: a counted city of eleven thousand, a fortress of four hundred, and a company of five, in that order of proximity and in no other. The figures are given without emphasis, the way a clerk reads out a schedule of assets.
e_a5_terms_1: Terms are agreed on the record in a socket chamber, in front of the crown clerk, with a Warden seal on the agreement and a Reckoning sister as witness. The payment schedule begins with the word immediately, which was in the terms, and which everybody heard, and which nobody thought to negotiate.
a5_price: The price is where the offer stops being abstract: one payment, taken at once, from the nearest principal. The door's own estimate of what that comes to has been written out in the crown ledger's tenth column in advance, in a clerk's hand, and the column has been ruled and waiting since the founding.
a5_price_a: A figure read in the tenth column of the crown ledger: a number of people and a date. It is written in the same neat hand as every other entry in the book, with the same abbreviations, in the same ink. It is the plainest sentence anybody has read in three books and it is four characters long.
a5_price_b: The question is asked about whether a smaller principal would serve, and it is answered in the affirmative, with a figure. The figure is five. It is given in the same tone as everything else, and the crown clerk writes it in the margin without being asked, because that is what he does with figures.
e_a5_price_1: The figure is refused, unread, which is the only genuinely cowardly decision available in this chamber. The company walks into the ring not knowing what it has been offered, and therefore unable to refuse it properly, and therefore unable to argue afterwards that it did not accept.
a5_oath: The last conversation before the ring is about the founders' oath, which Ashendrel offers in the founders' own form. That form is binding on it in a way nothing else in this mountain is, which is the whole reason the founders wrote it down. It requires a hand to swear on the other side.
a5_oath_a: An oath taken in the founders' own form, which the collar plate sets out and the crown ledger records. It binds both parties to terms neither can afterwards revise. It takes about a minute to say. Nobody in the chamber, including the crown clerk, has ever heard it said out loud before.
a5_oath_b: The oath refused and a Warden charter held up instead: a legal instrument of a state four hundred years old, addressed to an arrangement nine hundred years old, in a chamber that predates both. It is not a stupid decision. It is simply an instrument of the wrong jurisdiction, and everybody present knows it.
e_a5_oath_1: The founders' oath is taken by a sister of the Reckoning rather than by the captain, which is procedurally sound and which Nyre volunteers for before anybody can stop her. It makes her the party bound and not the company. She reads the form off the plate and gets every word of it right.
a5_stewards: The ring's working stewards are nine of the crown clerk's household on the ninth-hour rota, and they have kept the sockets, trimmed the lamps and packed the collars here for their whole working lives. They are unarmed. They are also the only people in the mountain who know which collar is due today.
a5_stewards_a: A charter put to nine stewards, who stand down formally, in writing, with the time entered. Then they stand in the gallery and watch, because they have nowhere else to be and the rota is at the ninth hour regardless of who is holding it, and somebody will have to do the collar work.
a5_stewards_b: One hour worked on the rota alongside nine stewards, trimming lamps and reading collars and passing lead. It teaches the company more about this door than the whole city archive did, and by the end of it the senior steward is explaining the eighth collar's crack without being asked anything at all.
a5_stewards_c: The question is asked and the collar man identified: a mason of sixty who has packed these collars for forty years. He knows what clause nine means in practice rather than in bronze, and he has never once been asked, and it takes him a moment to understand that the question is serious.
e_a5_stewards_1: A socket chamber is cleared by force of nine unarmed household stewards at the ninth hour. That leaves the ring unattended for the first time in nine hundred years, for eleven minutes. The rota's own margin, cut into the wall in the founders' hand, is nine, and the excess is where everything after this comes from.
e_a5_stewards_2: Nine stood-down stewards are sent out of the chamber entirely, which is correct procedure with civilians. It also removes from the room the only nine people who know which collar is due, on the day the eighth collar is due, in front of a company that has not read the rota's second page.
a5_legate: Prior Absolon Rell is here, in the socket chamber, having come up the wyrm-road ahead of the company with his coach left at Sarnhold. He has an appointment plate in his baggage. He greets the company by name and asks after their journey, and he is not surprised to see them and does not pretend to be.
a5_legate_a: A mother-house legate arrested in a socket chamber by a chartered company, in front of nine stewards, a crown clerk and a mason. All of them are willing to witness it. One of them writes it down, with the time, and asks the captain to sign the entry, which the captain does.
a5_legate_b: Rell's own account of his purpose, given without embarrassment: the office falls vacant in nine days, the mother house has resolved to fill it from within the order, and he is here to be appointed. He considers that a service. He explains, at some length, why he considers it a service.
e_a5_legate_1: A legate is allowed to proceed, and watched, which is the coldest decision available in this book. The appointment is properly made and correctly witnessed. The Reckoning holds the ninth hand of the crown door by nightfall, with a nine-year term and a household clause, and the company has minuted the whole thing.
a5_guild: Bruk Sunder is also here, with four delvers and a survey kit, entirely legally, on a Guild charter that predates the Warden charter by two hundred years. He has a copy of it with him. He offers it for inspection before anybody asks, which is the behaviour of a man who has read all of it.
a5_guild_a: A Guild charter read in full by two people who understand documents. It is genuine, older than the Wardens, and it grants mineral and salvage rights over precisely this chamber, in language that predates the Compact's own paperwork. There is no clause that excludes a living thing from the definition of a mineral deposit.
a5_guild_b: An order to leave is given to a Guild factor holding an older charter than yours, and he declines it courteously and has his delvers minute the exchange for the Guild's record. Then he goes back to his survey, and his survey is of the socket ring, and he is measuring the collars.
e_a5_guild_1: The question is asked of what the Guild intends, and answered fully, with figures. The Guild intends to work the arrangement as a going concern. It has costed it. It has a nine-year plan with the counted city as the labour supply, and Sunder produces the plan, and it is a good plan.
a5_rooks: Corrow's Rooks are in the gallery above the ring: eleven of them, chartered, armed, and working under a Warden commission that Thane did not mention because Thane did not issue it. They are not at the rail with the watchers. They are behind the watchers, spread out, covering the chamber's two doors.
a5_rooks_a: A fight in a socket chamber against eleven chartered mercenaries, in a room with nine warm sockets and a cracked collar in it. It is the worst possible place any of the twenty-two people present could have chosen, and every one of them knows it, and it happens anyway in the fourth minute.
a5_rooks_b: The masons' scaffold used to get above the gallery, which puts the company on the door frame looking down at eleven Rooks who have not thought about the roof. It takes four minutes. Corrow's lieutenant works it out on the third and cannot get his people turned round before the fourth.
a5_rooks_c: A commission produced and read: signed, sealed, and issued by the Reckoning's mother house under a Warden counter-seal that Rell carries in his own baggage. It makes the Rooks lawful. It also makes the company's charter contested, which is a thing that can be argued in a court and not in this chamber.
e_a5_rooks_1: A ring is held against eleven mercenaries coming down a gallery stair, which is good ground and the correct tactical choice. The eighth socket's cracked collar is nine feet behind the line. In the fourth minute somebody's whole weight goes into it, and the collar does what a cracked collar does.
e_a5_rooks_2: Eleven Rooks are pushed back up a gallery stair by a company that is winning, which is the point at which winning stops being useful. The stair leads to the tithe hall. The tithe hall is where the ninth-hour delivery is waiting to be called, and the calling has already started.
a5_die: The last works stand in the chamber's corner: the crown die on a portable anvil, brought down from the mint for the appointment, with a striker's hammer beside it and a blank already in the vice. The vice is a mason's vice. The blank has been filed and is ready for the tally to be cut.
a5_die_a: The crown die off its anvil and broken with a striker's hammer in four blows, in front of the crown clerk, the legate and the Guild. It ends the cutting of irons in this mountain permanently. Sunder objects on the record. The crown clerk does not object at all, and writes down the time.
a5_die_b: The blank in the vice, read with a lamp: founding gauge, crown tally, and a name already cut into the flank. It is the name Rell has been carrying an appointment plate for, cut in advance, in the mint's own hand, eleven days ago, which is the day the mint stopped cutting anything else.
e_a5_die_1: A blank is cut on the crown die by the captain's own hand, to see what happens, which is what the die is for. It produces a finished ninth iron with a name on its flank. The name is not one the cutter chose, and the die does not have a mechanism for choosing names.
a5_forge: The chamber's own small forge is kept for collar lead and iron work: hot, with a lead pot on it, a mason's tools laid out in order beside it, and a bench with nine years of chalk notes on the wall above it. Everything about it is the workshop of somebody who takes maintenance seriously.
a5_forge_a: An hour with a lead pot and a mason's tools, packing a cracked collar the way the rota specifies. It is not heroic in any way at all. It is also the thing most likely to keep this door shut for another century, and the mason works alongside the company and does not once take over.
a5_forge_b: The blank in the vice spoiled with a hot iron, deliberately and thoroughly, which cannot be undone. No appointment can be made in this chamber until the mint cuts another one, and the mint takes nine days to cut and the die is standing on an anvil four feet from the vice.
e_a5_forge_1: A founding-gauge crown iron is put into a working forge to see whether it will burn. It does not burn. It takes considerable exception to the attempt, in a chamber with eight of its fellows seated in the walls, and all eight of them take exception at the same moment and on the same count.
a5_wedge: The wedge has been Vurma's idea since Hollowmarch: an iron driven crosswise through the ring's collars rather than into a socket, locking all nine into one piece that no hand can draw and no keeper can count. She has drawn it three times on three different walls. She has the placement worked out.
a5_wedge_a: Vurma sets a wedge in the crown ring with forty years of Guild pathfinding behind the placement, which takes eleven minutes and two adjustments. It is the best piece of work anybody does in this book, and she does it in silence, and afterwards she puts her hand flat on it and leaves it there.
a5_wedge_b: A mason of forty years' collar experience checks the wedge's bearing before it is driven, which finds two problems and fixes both, and moves the wedge four inches to the left. He explains the reasoning while he works. Vurma listens to all of it and then thanks him, which she does not often do.
a5_wedge_c: A wedge set fast by the captain's own hands before the legate can object. It holds. Nobody in the chamber will certify it as sound, because nobody was allowed to look at it before it went in, and Vurma says exactly that, out loud, twice, and then does not mention it again.
e_a5_wedge_1: A chapel founding iron is used as the wedge, which is a different alloy cut in a different century for a different door. It shears under the ring's nine-count load in the fourth minute, with the whole company standing inside the ring, and the shearing takes the load with it into the collars.
e_a5_wedge_2: A second wedge is set on the far side of the ring for redundancy, which is sound engineering in every context except this one. It puts two hard points into a collar system designed to distribute its load across nine, and the ring's own count arrives at the pair of them from opposite directions.
a5_vigil: A dwarf watch-alcove opens off the socket chamber, where the stewards rest between rota hours: a bench, a lamp, a water jug and a clear view of the whole ring. Somebody has cut a tally into the bench's edge over the years, in nines, and stopped counting it about four hundred marks in.
a5_vigil_a: Three hours on a steward's bench with the ring in front of you and the company asleep in shifts around you. It is the last quiet anybody in this story gets, and everybody knows it at the time, and nobody wastes it talking. Kettle sleeps. Nyre does not. Nobody comments on either fact.
a5_masons: The masons on the scaffold at the door frame are a master of sixty, two journeymen and an apprentice, working on the frame's upper collar as they have every ninth day for forty years. They work steadily. They do not stop when the company comes in, and the master nods without taking his hand off the stone.
a5_masons_a: The master's answer about the frame, given in trade terms with his palm flat on the stone: the frame is spreading, has been spreading since autumn, and will need more than lead within the year. He has reported it four times. He has the copies of all four reports in his tool bag.
a5_masons_b: A mason of forty years asked what clause nine means in stone, and he answers: the founders cut this frame so that it fails inward rather than outward. He has spent his whole working life maintaining that failure. He explains what maintaining a failure means, and it takes him four sentences.
e_a5_masons_1: Four masons are ordered off a scaffold on a Warden charter in the middle of collar work, and they comply, because a charter is a charter. It leaves a partly-packed upper collar open on the day the eighth socket was already due, and the lead in the pot goes hard within the hour.
a5_scaffold: The masons' scaffold on the door frame is dwarf poles and planks, four levels of it, giving a hand's reach to the frame's upper collar and a clear view down into the socket ring. It has been up for forty years. Its lashings are renewed on a rota, and the rota is chalked on the bottom pole.
a5_scaffold_a: The upper collar seen at a hand's reach: dwarf stone, spread a finger's width, packed and repacked with lead in nine hundred years of visible layers like the rings of a tree. The newest layer is eleven days old, and the layer under it is nineteen years old, and the gap between them is the whole story.
a5_scaffold_b: The scaffold used as a route above the gallery, which nobody in the chamber expects because scaffolds are furniture. It gives the company the only high ground in a room that has been fought over exactly once before, in the founders' century, according to a note cut into the frame at scaffold height.
e_a5_scaffold_1: A masons' scaffold is taken down to deny it to other people, which takes forty minutes of honest work. It also removes the only access to an upper collar that is spreading a finger's width and is due for packing today, and the lead pot is on the forge, and the mason is standing beside it.
a5_crane: A dwarf crane stands over the ring, used for setting collar stone: a hook, a wire fall, a counterweight, and a bearing that is still greased and still turning after nine hundred years. It swings across the whole ring. There is a chalk mark on the floor showing where the counterweight sits when it is stowed.
a5_crane_a: The crane rigged to draw a collar stone under the mason's direction, which is exactly what it is for. It gives the company the ability to open or close the ring's stonework rather than only its irons, which is a different order of possibility and takes Ilsabet about four seconds to appreciate.
a5_crane_b: The crane rigged over the ninth socket, which is how the founders seated the first nine irons and how the ninth will be seated today by somebody. Rigging it puts that somebody's timing under the company's hand, and the legate watches the rigging from the desk without saying anything at all.
e_a5_crane_1: A nine-hundred-year-old counterweight is cut in a chamber with eight warm sockets and a scaffold in it. Eleven hundred pounds of dwarf stone arrives on the ring floor at the ninth minute, which is the minute the ring's own movement comes round, and the two of those things together are what the founders' rota exists to prevent.
a5_seal: The founders' seal is cut into the chamber floor in front of the ring: nine hands in a circle around a door, and around them an inscription in the founders' own hand. The counted city has never translated it. It has been walked over by every keeper, steward and mason for nine hundred years.
a5_seal_a: A founders' inscription translated on a chamber floor after nine hundred years, by a hedge-thaumaturge kneeling on it with a lamp. It is not a dedication and not a warning. It is an apology, addressed to whoever is standing on it, from the people who built the arrangement, and it names what they did.
e_a5_seal_1: A founders' seal is cut out of the chamber floor and carried, because it is the only apology anybody ever wrote for any of this. It is nine hundred pounds of dwarf flagstone. The company cannot get it up the wyrm-road, and the attempt takes four hours, and the four hours were the margin.
a5_watchers: In the gallery above the ring, nine of the counted stand at the rail in shifts and watch the door. They have watched it in shifts, without instruction from anybody living, for nine hundred years. They are not guards. They have no weapons. They are simply always there, nine of them, and the shift changes on the hour.
a5_watchers_a: The answer given by nine people at a rail: they are watching for the day the count stops. The founders told the first nine to watch. Each nine has told the next nine since. Nobody has ever stood them down, and no keeper has ever tried, and they are not entirely sure the keeper could.
a5_watchers_b: Nine watchers got out of the gallery before the ninth hour, with some difficulty and a good deal of patient argument. It is a kindness. It also means that for the first time in nine hundred years nobody is at the rail when the hour comes, and the rail is what the watching was from.
a5_watchers_c: One full shift stood at the rail with nine of the counted, in silence, watching a door breathe on a nine-count. It is the single most useful hour of preparation available in this chamber, and at the end of it the eldest watcher tells the company what changes in the rhythm before the hour turns.
e_a5_watchers_1: A gallery is cleared by force because it is a firing position, and nine watchers are put out of a place they have held in shifts for nine hundred years. On the way out the ninth of them explains, without rancour, what they were watching for and what they were told to do when they saw it.
e_a5_watchers_2: The watchers are asked what they were told to do if the count stopped, and all nine of them answer at once, in the founders' own words, which they have had by heart since childhood. The words are an instruction. The company is standing inside the instruction while they say it.
a5_hollow: Vurma's hammer finds a hollow behind the ring wall: a void the founders left between the door frame and the rock, with a dwarf ladder in it and nine hundred years of undisturbed dust on the ladder's rungs. The access plate comes away in her hands, and it was made to come away in somebody's hands.
a5_hollow_a: The founders' ladder descended into a void nobody has entered since the founding. At the bottom there is a bench, a tool rack with its tools still in it, and a set of written instructions on the wall in nine bronze plates. The instructions are for dismantling the door, and they are complete.
a5_hollow_b: The void sounded and mapped from outside with a hammer and a wire, which tells Vurma its size and shape and one further fact: the door's frame is not attached to the rock in the way the entire counted city believes it is. She says that twice, and the second time she says what it means.
a5_hollow_c: Kettle down the founders' ladder alone with a lamp, and back in eleven minutes, white. She describes a bench, a tool rack and a set of instructions in dwarf that she cannot read. Ilsabet can. Kettle also says that the dust down there has one set of footprints in it, and they are not hers.
e_a5_hollow_1: A founders' hollow is walled up to keep it from other people, with the company on the outside of it. That seals the only route by which the door could ever be dismantled, and the only apparatus for doing it, and the instructions for how. It takes two hours and it is entirely irreversible.
e_a5_hollow_2: A set of nine-hundred-year-old dismantling instructions is taken off a founders' wall and carried up a ladder: nine bronze plates, forty pounds. The plates are the wall's own bracing. The founders fixed the instructions to the thing they were instructions for, which is either a joke or a precaution.
a5_bellows: A dwarf bellows apparatus stands in the hollow, connected through the rock to the door's own frame, built by the founders for a purpose the crown clerk has never known about. The masons know. It is on their rota, once every ninth decade, and the rota's page for it has been blank for ninety years.
a5_bellows_a: The mason's explanation, given with real pleasure at being asked a professional question: the bellows cools the frame's upper collar. It has not been worked in ninety years, because the rota went out of use when the last master died. Working it now would buy this frame a decade, possibly more.
a5_bellows_b: The bellows worked by two people for an hour, in a stone void, by lamplight, in silence. It drops the upper collar's temperature by a measurable amount and tightens the frame's spread by a hair. It is the most boring act of heroism in three books and it is unambiguously the most useful.
e_a5_bellows_1: A founders' bellows is left alone on the principle that the founders left it there for a reason, which is true. The reason is that it must be worked every ninth decade. This is the ninetieth year, which is written on the plate above it, in the founders' hand, in figures.
a5_tithebox: The tithe box beside the ring is a dwarf strongbox where the counted city's tokens are collected after each delivery. It is full: nine hundred years of tokens, each one a household's name on a disc of fired clay. There is a tally slate on the lid, and the slate is written up to today.
a5_tithebox_a: The tally slate read off the strongbox lid: this month's tokens, next month's requirement, and a note in the crown clerk's hand recording that the requirement has doubled since Kar Duhn shut. Under that, in the same hand, a second note recording that it doubled again after Hollowmarch.
a5_tithebox_b: A dwarf strongbox of nine hundred years of household tokens taken and lashed to the barrow: ninety pounds of fired clay and the counted city's entire record of who paid what and when. Each token has a name on it. Nyre insists on carrying it herself for the first mile and then admits she cannot.
e_a5_tithebox_1: Nine hundred years of household tokens are emptied into a founders' hollow to destroy the record. The record was the only proof that any of the eleven thousand ever paid anything. The city's arithmetic simply starts again from one the following morning, and everybody's arrears are recalculated from a clean sheet.
a5_decision: The ring at the ninth hour, with everything now known. Eight irons warm and one socket bright and empty. A crown iron somewhere in the room. A legate with an appointment plate, a Guild with an older charter, eleven Rooks on the stair, nine watchers at a rail, and a door breathing on a nine-count in front of five people.
